name: Ancient Greek
blurb: The language of Plato, Sophocles and Thucydides, and the source of words from democracy to zoology.
facts: Greek has a written record of about 3,400 years, from Mycenaean palace tablets in Linear B to today's newspapers.
The Greeks borrowed their letters from the Phoenicians around 800 BC and turned spare consonant signs into vowels.
Athens officially switched to the 24-letter Ionic alphabet in 403 BC. Before that, E also stood for η and O for ω.
Plato wrote only capitals, with no accents or spaces. Accents arrived around 200 BC, small letters around AD 800.
The accent was pitch, not stress. One ancient writer says the voice rose by about a musical fifth.
Athenian silver coins, the famous 'owls', carry the letters ΑΘΕ, short for 'of the Athenians'.

guide.p: Many capitals look Latin, but some fool you: Η is ē, Ρ is r, Χ is ch. Classical Athenians wrote only capitals. Small letters came in the Middle Ages.
A word starting with a vowel carries a little hook. ἀ (smooth) adds nothing, ἁ (rough) adds an h. A word starting with ρ always has the rough one.
ά ὰ ᾶ mark where the voice rose or fell in pitch. Notice them, but you never have to type them.
γγ is ng. υ is y, but after α, ε or ο it is u. The tiny iota under ᾳ ῃ ῳ was pronounced in classical times, so type it as i.
Sigma is σ inside a word and ς at the end.

items.note: Before γ, κ, ξ or χ it sounds n: ἄγγελος, angelos.

units.title: Chaire
units.about: Greet people and say who they are

guide.p: χαῖρε is literally 'rejoice!' or 'be well', said both on meeting and on parting. To a group: χαίρετε.
Put ὦ before the person you address. Names and nouns in -ος switch to -ε: φίλος becomes φίλε. Speakers in the assembly and the law courts addressed the crowd as ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι.
εἰμί 'I am', εἶ 'you are', ἐστίν 'he, she or it is'. Greek has no word for 'a': φίλος is 'a friend'.
οὐ before a consonant, οὐκ before a smooth breathing, οὐχ before a rough one. After οὐκ, ἐστίν is written ἔστιν. On its own, 'no!' is οὔ.
εἰμί and ἐστίν lean on the word before them and can lose their accent or push an extra one onto it. That is why you will see ἄνθρωπός εἰμι.

items.note: Also used for goodbye. To a group: χαίρετε.

units.title: Oikia
units.about: Family, home and the word for 'the'

guide.p: Unlike Latin, Greek has a word for 'the': ὁ for masculine nouns, ἡ for feminine, τό for neuter. Learn every noun with it, because it tells you the gender. There is still no 'a'.
As the object, -ος becomes -ον, -η becomes -ην, -α becomes -αν, and the article becomes τόν, τήν, τό. Neuter nouns look the same either way. Word order is free.
καλός, καλή, καλόν: the ending follows the noun's gender. Saying 'X is beautiful', the adjective takes no article.
An acute on the last syllable turns grave when another word follows: ἀδελφός, but ὁ ἀδελφὸς καὶ ἡ ἀδελφή.

τίς is 'who?' and τί 'what?'. They always keep their acute. ἆρα at the start turns a statement into a yes-or-no question. Printed Greek uses ; as its question mark.

units.title: Gnōthi seauton
units.about: Famous lines and where they come from

guide.p: γνῶθι 'know!', ἄειδε 'sing!' and ἔννεπε 'tell!' are orders. With a command, 'not' is μή, so 'nothing' is μηδέν.
γνῶθι σεαυτόν and μηδὲν ἄγαν were inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi. Plato (Protagoras 343b) says the Seven Sages dedicated them there. He writes the shorter Attic form, γνῶθι σαυτόν.

The Iliad opens μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά, the Odyssey ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, Μοῦσα. The object comes first. ἄνδρα is ἀνήρ as an object, μοι is 'to me'. Homer's Greek is an older, mixed dialect, not Attic: an Athenian said ᾆδε for ἄειδε.
ex: tell me of the man, Muse

guide.p: Neuter plurals end in -α and take the article τά. Greek can leave out 'are'.

θάλαττα θάλαττα: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.7.24, as the Ten Thousand sight the Black Sea. εὕρηκα: Archimedes in his bath, told by the Roman Vitruvius two centuries later. πάντα ῥεῖ is a later summary of Heraclitus, not in his surviving words; Plato (Cratylus 402a) has him say that everything moves on and nothing stays. χαλεπὰ τὰ καλά is an old proverb Plato quotes (Republic 435c). The last line is Aristotle, Politics 1253a, where φύσει means 'by nature'.

units.title: Ēlthon
units.about: Tell a story in the past

guide.p: Greek's main past tense is the aorist. It reports an event as one complete whole: 'I wrote', 'she fled'. It is the tense of storytelling.
Past tenses put ἐ- in front of the verb. With a prefix such as ἀπο- 'away', the augment goes after the prefix: ἀπ-έ-θανεν.

Most verbs add σ and the endings -α 'I', -ας 'you', -ε(ν) 'he, she or it'. The σ blends with the consonant before it: π or φ with σ gives ψ, κ or χ with σ gives ξ. Verbs in -άω lengthen their vowel: νικάω, ἐνίκησα. The ν of -εν is optional, usually written before a vowel or a pause.

Some common verbs change their stem instead and take the endings -ον, -ες, -ε(ν): φεύγω 'I flee', ἔφυγον 'I fled'. A few borrow a different verb altogether: the past of λέγω is εἶπον, 'I saw' is εἶδον and 'I went' is ἦλθον.
ἦν is 'he, she or it was', or 'there was'. It is the past of ἐστίν, but it never leans on the word before it.
Plutarch (Caesar 50) says Caesar reported a lightning victory in three words, and gives them in Greek: ἦλθον, εἶδον, ἐνίκησα.

units.title: Basileus
units.about: Kings, bodies and nouns that change their stem

guide.p: Many nouns hide their stem in the nominative, and the other cases add endings to a longer stem: σῶμα 'body', stem σωματ-; παῖς 'boy', stem παιδ-. As an object, a masculine or feminine noun usually takes -α: τὸν παῖδα, τὴν νύκτα. A few, like πόλις, take -ν instead: τὴν πόλιν.

The genitive means 'of'. The article becomes τοῦ for masculine and neuter nouns and τῆς for feminine ones. Nouns in -ος switch to -ου, nouns in -η to -ης, nouns in -α to -ας or -ης, and the third declension adds -ος to the stem: σώματος, παιδός.
Dictionaries list the nominative and the genitive, because the genitive shows the stem: σῶμα, σώματος. πόλις and nouns in -ευς have a genitive in -εως: πόλις, πόλεως; βασιλεύς, βασιλέως.

In the plural the article is οἱ, αἱ, τά. Nouns in -ος end in -οι, nouns in -η or -α in -αι, and third-declension nouns in -ες, or -α if neuter. 'They are' is εἰσίν. Every plural genitive ends in -ων: τῶν Ἑλλήνων 'of the Greeks'.
ἄρχω 'I rule' puts what is ruled in the genitive: ἄρχει τῆς πόλεως, literally 'he rules of the city'.

units.title: Boulomai
units.about: Wanting, becoming and the middle voice

guide.p: Beside active and passive, Greek verbs have a middle voice, which shows the subject acting on or for itself: παύω 'I stop (someone)', παύομαι 'I stop, I cease'. Its endings are -ομαι, -ει, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται.
Many common verbs exist only in the middle but have ordinary active meanings: βούλομαι 'I want', ἔρχομαι 'I come', μάχομαι 'I fight'. Grammars call them deponents. 'You want' is βούλει.
The infinitive ends in -ειν in the active and -εσθαι in the middle: γράφειν 'to write', γίγνεσθαι 'to become'. βούλομαι takes an infinitive, just like English 'want to'.
ex: I want to hear the speech

guide.p: The middle aorist has the augment and the endings -όμην 'I', -ου 'you', -ετο 'he, she or it': ἐγενόμην 'I became', ἐγένετο 'he became' or 'it happened'.
In the Athenian assembly the herald opened debate with τίς ἀγορεύειν βούλεται; Aeschines (Against Timarchus 23) says the oldest citizens were invited first, then everyone else.

units.title: Legōn
units.about: Participles: doing two things at once

guide.p: A participle is a verb used as an adjective: λέγων 'saying', φεύγων 'fleeing'. It agrees with its noun. The present active runs -ων, -ουσα, -ον, and the masculine object form is -οντα.
ex: I saw the wolf running away

guide.p: Greek uses a participle where English adds a second clause. The present means 'while ...ing', the aorist 'after ...ing'. The aorist participle drops the augment: εἶδον, ἰδών; εἶπον, εἰπών; ἤκουσα, ἀκούσας.
ex: having said this, he went away
ὁ λύκος τὸν κύνα ἰδὼν ἔφυγεν
on seeing the dog, the wolf fled

guide.p: With the article a participle becomes a noun: ὁ λέγων 'the one speaking, the speaker'. Athenian law let ὁ βουλόμενος, 'anyone who wishes', bring a prosecution on behalf of someone wronged.
The participle of εἰμί is ὤν, οὖσα, ὄν 'being'. Thucydides (4.78) has the Spartan general Brasidas say he came φίλος ὤν, 'as a friend'.
παύομαι 'I stop' takes a participle for what you stop doing. Middle participles end in -όμενος, -ομένη, -όμενον: βουλόμενος 'wanting'.

guide.p: The dative means 'to' or 'for' someone. The article is τῷ, τῇ, τῷ and the noun ends in -ῳ, -ῃ or -ᾳ, or -ι in the third declension. In the plural: τοῖς, ταῖς with -οις, -αις or -σι.
ex: I sent a letter to my friend

guide.p: ἐκ 'out of' and ἀπό 'away from' take the genitive, ἐν 'in' takes the dative, εἰς 'into' the accusative. Roughly: motion away, the genitive; rest, the dative; motion towards, the accusative. ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel.

Some prepositions change meaning with the case. μετά is 'with' with the genitive, 'after' with the accusative. παρά is 'from' a person with the genitive, 'beside' with the dative, 'to' a person with the accusative. διά is 'through' with the genitive, 'because of' with the accusative.
As plural objects, nouns in -ος end in -ους, nouns in -η or -α in -ας, and third-declension nouns in -ας. The article is τούς, τάς, τά.
εἷς, μία, ἕν 'one' and τρεῖς, τρία 'three' change with gender. From five upwards numbers never change. Greeks also wrote numbers with letters: α is 1, β is 2, ι is 10.
οἱ ἑπτὰ σοφοί were wise men of the 6th century BC, among them Solon of Athens and Thales of Miletus. Plato names them in the Protagoras (343a).

guide.p: The future adds σ to the stem and takes the present endings: γράφω 'I write', γράψω 'I will write'. The σ blends with consonants as in the aorist, but there is no augment.
Some verbs have a middle future even when their present is active: ὁράω 'I see', ὄψομαι 'I will see'. 'I will be' is ἔσομαι, and 'he, she or it will be' is ἔσται.
ὅτι 'that' reports what someone says and keeps the tense of the original words. ἐπεί means 'when' or 'since'.

guide.p: Greek loves balance. μέν marks the first half of a contrast and δέ the second. Neither can start a clause, so they come second. ὁ μέν ... ὁ δέ means 'one ... the other'.
ex: ὁ μὲν γράφει, ὁ δὲ λέγει
